title: Despair, Hope, and a Cry for Justice
overview: Written after Babylon destroyed Jerusalem, this poem (built on the Hebrew alphabet, three verses for each letter) follows one sufferer from feeling hunted by God, to fragile hope in his mercy, to grief and a plea for justice.

parts.label: Feeling hunted by God (vv. 1-18)
parts.note: A man describes his suffering as if God were his enemy: a bear in ambush, an archer taking aim, a jailer who walls him in and shuts out his prayers. Tradition names him Jeremiah, but the poem does not, and scholars are unsure whether he is one person or a voice for the whole ruined people.

parts.label: Choosing to remember (vv. 19-24)
parts.note: Remembering his pain drags him down, yet he deliberately calls to mind that God's loyal love and mercies are renewed every morning, and that God himself is his portion, the share a person inherits (v. 24). Translations differ in verse 22: the two here say this love is why the people are not wiped out, while others render it as the love itself never ending.

parts.label: Quiet waiting (vv. 25-30)
parts.note: The tone turns to calm advice: wait quietly for God, bear a yoke (a heavy burden) while young, sit silent with face in the dust as a sign of humility, even accept a blow on the cheek. Christians later read verse 30 alongside Jesus' teaching on turning the other cheek and his own suffering.

parts.label: Why suffering is not the end (vv. 31-39)
parts.note: God does not reject anyone forever and takes no pleasure in causing grief. When prisoners are crushed and justice is twisted, translations differ on whether the text says God sees it or does not approve of it (vv. 34-36). Then comes a hard claim: both disaster and good come from God, so why should the living complain when punished for their sins (vv. 37-39)?

parts.label: Confession without relief (vv. 40-51)
parts.note: The voice turns to 'we': the people resolve to examine themselves and admit their sin, yet say bluntly that God has not forgiven, has killed without pity, and hides behind a cloud no prayer can get through (vv. 40-47). The speaker then weeps without stopping for his destroyed people, until God looks down and sees (vv. 48-51).

parts.label: From the pit to a plea (vv. 52-66)
parts.note: Hunted like a bird and left in a pit with water over his head, he called on God, who came near and told him not to be afraid. Scholars debate whether this recalls a past rescue or prays for one (vv. 52-58). He ends by asking God to repay, curse and destroy his enemies, though translations differ on whether verses 64 to 66 are a prayer or a prediction.

disagreement: Christians differ on how to read the chapter's insistence that suffering comes from God's own hand (vv. 1-18, 37-38): some take it as teaching that God actively sends hardship as just discipline, while others read it as the honest perception of someone in grief, or as God allowing what he does not directly cause.
think: Can a person hold on to some hope while still saying honestly that things are terrible, or does one always end up crowding out the other?
